articles.title: Unprecedented images may explain one of greatest mysteries of the sun

chapters.label: 【篇章1】

paras.en: The image of the sun’s surface, taken by the Inouye solar telescope, reveals signatures of what scientists call Kelvin-Helmholtz instabilities. Photograph: NSF/NSO/Aura/MPS View image in fullscreen The image of the sun’s surface, taken by the Inouye solar telescope, reveals signatures of what scientists call Kelvin-Helmholtz instabilities. Photograph: NSF/NSO/Aura/MPS The sun Unprecedented images may explain one of greatest mysteries of the sun Highest-ever resolution pictures of our star could help show why its corona is millions of degrees hotter than its surface Prefer the Guardian on Google Golden bands and swirling vortices have been spotted on the sun in the most detailed images ever captured of the turbulent surface of our home star. Astronomers observed the sun with the Inouye solar telescope in Hawaii, the world’s most powerful solar telescope, and saw new features smaller than 20km (12 miles) across in a magnetically active region close to a sun spot. The unprecedented pictures show processes on the surface that are likely to explain the decades-long mystery of why the corona, the sun’s outer atmosphere, is millions of degrees hotter than its surface. The most high-res image of the sun “These are the highest spatial resolution images of the solar surface ever acquired,” said Dr Friedrich Wöger, a senior scientist at the US National Solar Observatory, which operates the telescope near the summit of the Haleakalā volcano, on the island of Maui. Previous observations with the telescope found the sun’s surface to be a patchwork of granular structures each about the size of France. Those images picked out details as small as 30km across, but the latest are right at the limit of the telescope’s capability. View image in fullscreen Images of the sun’s surface taken in early 2020.

Photograph: NSO/Aura/NSF “My first reaction was: ‘Wow, how can we see such tiny, fine-scale structures on the sun?” said Dr David Kuridze, an astronomer on the team. “This is something we have never seen before in any solar observations.” In the latest images, the small whirlpool-like structures on the sun’s surface were identified as signatures of what scientists call Kelvin-Helmholtz instabilities (KHIs). These form when fast-moving plasma slides past slower moving fluid, creating shear at the interface. This sets up small disturbances in the sun’s plasma that grow into spiralling vortices that look like breaking waves. Scientists have seen KHIs in lakes and oceans, and in cloud formations on Earth, and even in the atmospheres of Jupiter and Saturn, but have never confirmed their existence on the sun. The details of the findings are published in Nature . Explosive events on the sun, from solar flares and jets to coronal mass ejections, are powered by extreme, fluctuating magnetic fields in the star. The explosions can cause widespread disruption on Earth, taking out power grids, satellites, GPS positioning and global communications. View image in fullscreen A magnified area of one of the latest images of the sun’s surface. Photograph: NSF/NSO/Aura/MPS The magnetic fields are generated by the movement of hot, charged plasma in the sun, but the physics isn’t fully understood. Astronomers know that magnetic field lines can twist around each other like braided hair, creating tension that is suddenly released when the tangled lines break. What is less clear is what starts the process. The swirling vortices are now a key culprit, explaining why the field lines become braided in the first place, and perhaps why the sun’s corona is heated to a few million degrees while the surface is a mere 6,000C.

“This could solve this biggest mystery of the last half a century for solar physics and astrophysics,” said Kuridze. “When you have this instability in the system, it is very easy to cascade the energy into smaller scales. And at some point, it just dissipates as a heat. This could make hot coronas, hot outer atmospheres of the sun and similar stars.”

articles.title: Teachers need help with AI. A union is offering training – with $23m in funding from big tech

chapters.label: 【篇章1】

paras.en: Without guidance from their schools or districts, many teachers are left to figure out whether and how to use AI tools. Composite: Rita Liu/The Guardian/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Without guidance from their schools or districts, many teachers are left to figure out whether and how to use AI tools. Composite: Rita Liu/The Guardian/Getty Images Reworked Schools Teachers need help with AI. A union is offering training – with $23m in funding from big tech Partnership between American Federation of Teachers, one of the largest labor unions in the US, and AI firms has stirred controversy About this content Lee V Gaines Wed 5 Aug 2026 13. 00 BST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google D arius Saczuk, a high school teacher, views artificial intelligence as his enemy. Earlier this year, he and several dozen New York City teachers spent the day inside a windowless conference room in downtown Manhattan to learn how to use AI and prevent students from outsourcing their thinking to it. As Saczuk sees it, he needs to understand his enemy in order to beat it. “It’s killing our jobs, it’s changing our society, it’s replacing humans,” said Saczuk, who teaches English as a new language at Long Island City high school in Queens. “In order to retain my job, I need to know how to use AI because it’s not going away.” So he turned to training offered by the American Federation of Teachers, one of the largest labor unions in the US with roughly 1. 8 million members, at its new National Academy for AI Instruction. Last year, the academy began offering in-person and virtual AI training across the country.

The goal is to train 400,000 educators over the span of five years, helping them understand AI’s benefits and potential harms and also shape how it’s used in the classroom. Without guidance from their schools or districts, many teachers are left to figure out whether and how to use AI tools. Though the AFT’s $23m training initiative is one of the few structured programs for teachers, its funding, provided entirely by Microsoft, OpenAI and Anthropic, is stirring controversy. Supporters say the training is necessary for the future, but critics argue the academy pushes AI into classrooms, steering teachers toward tools that undermine students’ learning. “It’s handing more political power over” to big tech, said Audrey Watters, author of Teaching Machines: The History of Personalized Learning. It’s really “dangerous” for educators to partner with companies that “seem opposed” to the goal of education, she said. AI has become a ubiquitous force in classrooms, despite the lack of official guidance. More than half of polled teens say they use AI for help with schoolwork and nearly six in 10 think using AI to cheat is a regular occurrence at their schools, according to a Pew Research Center survey conducted last fall. Meanwhile only about four in 10 teachers say their schools offer professional development or training related to AI, according to a recent NPR/Ipsos poll . And about half of all teachers polled say their school hasn’t offered any guidance on AI, or they’re unclear on what it is. Teaching educators about AI is a “moral imperative”, said Randi Weingarten, the AFT president. She argues that AI training empowers teachers to make informed decisions about how, when or whether to use AI in their instruction.

And without outside funding, it was a choice between taking big yech’s money or doing nothing, she said. “There was no fairy godmother philanthropist that was sprinkling millions of dollars on us to actually create a mechanism to educate,” Weingarten said. “I am not promoting the use of AI. Educators need to know the tool.” For Microsoft, which is contributing the largest share of funding at $12. 5m, the goal is to give educators a voice in shaping how AI products are used, said Justin Spelhaug, leader of Microsoft’s education, workforce and nonprofit programs. “By partnering with teachers’ unions … we believe we can learn directly from teachers on what they want and need in their classroom,” he said in a statement. But Watters asserts that AI’s presence in the classroom is not a foregone conclusion. “The industry would very much like us to believe that it’s not going away,” Watters said. “But the future is unwritten.” Tech company leaders have largely painted AI as beneficial to education, some even claiming AI could replace teachers . But experts say there’s still a lack of research proving whether AI actually improves learning outcomes. In a 2024 blog post , Sam Altman, the OpenAI CEO, said he envisioned a future where “children will have virtual tutors”. AI could replicate some of the meaningful experiences teachers provide, such as making students feel understood and inspired, Greg Brockman, the OpenAI president, said in 2023 on the Possible podcast , hosted by Reid Hoffman, the LinkedIn co-founder, and Aria Finger, his chief of staff. View image in fullscreen The Khanmigo chatbot, an AI-powered guide developed by Khan Academy, is seen during a math and science class at Khan Lab School in Palo Alto, California.

chapters.label: 【篇章2】

paras.en: Photograph: The Washington Post/Getty Images “Imagine if you could give that kind of teacher to every student 24/7 … for free,” Brockman said. Microsoft believes “AI can help reduce administrative burdens, personalize learning and create more time for students”, Spelhaug said. “But there is no substitute for the role of a teacher.” OpenAI, which pledged $10m to the academy, and Anthropic, which committed $500,000 to the first year, did not respond to a request for comment. AI companies are already making their way into classrooms. Over the last two years, Miami-Dade county public schools, one of the largest US districts, began rolling out Google’s Gemini chatbot to teachers and high school students . Last fall, Microsoft announced AI tools for teachers at no additional cost for educational customers. And OpenAI and Anthropic offer K-12 teachers free use of versions of their chatbots designed for educators. There’s been a longstanding playbook in which tech companies provide free training and resources to teachers in exchange for feedback and product advocacy, said Justin Reich, a Massachusetts Institute of Technology professor and author of Failure to Disrupt: Why Technology Alone Can’t Transform Education. Google, for example, entrenched itself in schools by offering districts free or low-cost educational software for classroom laptops. It’s also built a corps of Google Certified Educators, teachers trained on the company’s software who promote it to their peers. Last year, Google introduced free Gemini certifications for K-12 teachers and students as young as 13. But the aim is profits, Reich said. “Their goal is to get people to become lifelong consumers,” he said. Still, “there’s no evidence that the adoption of Google or Microsoft products lead to better outcomes, happier teachers, more efficient school systems or anything”. The AFT’s new academy seems to echo Google’s approach, Watters said.

By offering training through a labor union, viewed as a peer group, tech companies make their AI products seem more credible, she said. “It feels very different to have your union say, ‘We’re offering a training,’ than it does to have a company say [it],” Watters said. The concern is “understandable” though not accurate, Spelhaug said. “This initiative was designed in response to a need our union partners and educators themselves identified,” he said. “Our role is to provide resources and expertise while respecting the independence of the AFT and the professional judgment of teachers.” The AFT doesn’t allow companies to promote products during the sessions, Weingarten said. And while she doesn’t think “students have to use AI in schools”, she believes educators cannot ignore what’s already here. View image in fullscreen Pilar Cuevas, a social studies teacher, looks up at her interactive whiteboard during her class in Inglewood, California. Cuevas gives her students homework in a Cornell notes format, which makes it more difficult for them to input their homework into an AI program. Photograph: Juliana Yamada/Los Angeles Times/Getty Images In a May speech at the National Press Club, Weingarten called for a ban on student-facing AI in elementary schools and said the AFT is working with Microsoft, OpenAI and Anthropic on a “gold standard” for AI safety and privacy in schools. If the companies don’t deliver on the promise, the union will walk away from the funding, she added. “They have agreed in concept,” she said. “But until the Is are dotted and the Ts are crossed, there’s no agreement.” Microsoft didn’t share any details or timeline about new standards, but Spelhaug said the company shares the AFT’s goal. There’s no established approach for training teachers on AI. The technology is simply too new.

But the academy’s leaders hope to work with teachers to find ways to use the technology without compromising students’ cognitive development, independent thinking, data privacy and mental health. “The sad thing is there is no map, and the terrain is changing every single day,” John Holleran, an AI academy trainer said to teachers assembled at a May session. “So, it’s going to be difficult for us to sort of figure out where we’re going.” Demand for the academy’s training is strong. A May training sold out within hours, leaving about 150 people on the waitlist, according to staff. The session focused on two key points: AI can’t replace teachers. And it can’t be blindly trusted because it can be biased or hallucinate, meaning make things up. For example, ChatGPT generated an image of a white man in a suit and tie when asked to show a successful person – a bias Holleran said teachers need to be aware of when creating prompts. Several teachers at the training said AI is already helping them tackle classroom challenges. Phillip Perry, who teaches ninth grade at Bronx High School for Law and Community Service, uses AI to design lessons for students with disabilities. “Trying to differentiate instruction in a way that can completely target their learning needs has been a massive challenge,” Perry said. “Using AI is helpful in breaking down tasks to the smallest form to help build the students up as they go.” Tanushree Sengupta, a math teacher at Hillcrest high school in Queens, uses AI to generate practice math problems and, eventually, to analyze student data and flag those needing extra support or a challenge. But she worries that the tech could be a crutch.

“I need to figure out ways where [students are] doing more thinking that they can actually show,” she said, adding that she signed up for the training in part to help students think for themselves. To that end, AFT trainers advised teachers to redesign their curriculum to favor student-led discussions, journaling and thought exercises that require human judgement and reasoning. The training filled a void, offering practical strategies for the classroom, said Perry and Sengupta, who were unaware of the academy’s funding prior to speaking to the Guardian. “As long as what they’re providing is beneficial to the students and the teachers, then I don’t see an issue,” Perry said. Saczuk, the teacher from Queens, considered the training “necessary”. Still, he left with more questions than answers. “What is the role of the teacher?” he asked. “It’s a big question mark.”

Google, for example, entrenched itself in schools by offering districts free or low-cost educational software for classroom laptops. It’s also built a corps of Google Certified Educators, teachers trained on the company’s software who promote it to their peers. Last year, Google introduced free Gemini certifications for K-12 teachers and students as young as 13. But the aim is profits, Reich said. “Their goal is to get people to become lifelong consumers,” he said. Still, “there’s no evidence that the adoption of Google or Microsoft products lead to better outcomes, happier teachers, more efficient school systems or anything”. The AFT’s new academy seems to echo Google’s approach, Watters said.

By offering training through a labor union, viewed as a peer group, tech companies make their AI products seem more credible, she said. “It feels very different to have your union say, ‘We’re offering a training,’ than it does to have a company say [it],” Watters said. The concern is “understandable” though not accurate, Spelhaug said. “This initiative was designed in response to a need our union partners and educators themselves identified,” he said. “Our role is to provide resources and expertise while respecting the independence of the AFT and the professional judgment of teachers.” The AFT doesn’t allow companies to promote products during the sessions, Weingarten said. And while she doesn’t think “students have to use AI in schools”, she believes educators cannot ignore what’s already here. View image in fullscreen Pilar Cuevas, a social studies teacher, looks up at her interactive whiteboard during her class in Inglewood, California. Cuevas gives her students homework in a Cornell notes format, which makes it more difficult for them to input their homework into an AI program. Photograph: Juliana Yamada/Los Angeles Times/Getty Images In a May speech at the National Press Club, Weingarten called for a ban on student-facing AI in elementary schools and said the AFT is working with Microsoft, OpenAI and Anthropic on a “gold standard” for AI safety and privacy in schools. If the companies don’t deliver on the promise, the union will walk away from the funding, she added. “They have agreed in concept,” she said. “But until the Is are dotted and the Ts are crossed, there’s no agreement.” Microsoft didn’t share any details or timeline about new standards, but Spelhaug said the company shares the AFT’s goal. And it can’t be blindly trusted because it can be biased or hallucinate, meaning make things up. For example, ChatGPT generated an image of a white man in a suit and tie when asked to show a successful person – a bias Holleran said teachers need to be aware of when creating prompts. Several teachers at the training said AI is already helping them tackle classroom challenges. Phillip Perry, who teaches ninth grade at Bronx High School for Law and Community Service, uses AI to design lessons for students with disabilities. “Trying to differentiate instruction in a way that can completely target their learning needs has been a massive challenge,” Perry said. “Using AI is helpful in breaking down tasks to the smallest form to help build the students up as they go.” Tanushree Sengupta, a math teacher at Hillcrest high school in Queens, uses AI to generate practice math problems and, eventually, to analyze student data and flag those needing extra support or a challenge. But she worries that the tech could be a crutch.

“I need to figure out ways where [students are] doing more thinking that they can actually show,” she said, adding that she signed up for the training in part to help students think for themselves. To that end, AFT trainers advised teachers to redesign their curriculum to favor student-led discussions, journaling and thought exercises that require human judgement and reasoning. The training filled a void, offering practical strategies for the classroom, said Perry and Sengupta, who were unaware of the academy’s funding prior to speaking to the Guardian. “As long as what they’re providing is beneficial to the students and the teachers, then I don’t see an issue,” Perry said. articles.title: ‘Leicester Square, please guv’: Self-driving taxis cleared for London streets ‘later this summer’

chapters.label: 【篇章1】

paras.en: A Wayve autonomous car on a London street. Photograph: Wayve View image in fullscreen A Wayve autonomous car on a London street. Photograph: Wayve Self-driving cars ‘Leicester Square, please guv’: Self-driving taxis cleared for London streets ‘later this summer’ Wayve Uber wins first minicab licence for autonomous cabs from TfL but vehicles will have a safety driver (at first) Prefer the Guardian on Google The taxi app company Uber and the autonomous technology developer Wayve have been granted the first minicab licences in London allowing them to offer self-driving taxi rides to paying customers – but with a human safety driver in place, for now. The companies said they would start trips in the UK “later this summer” before the full public launch. The San Francisco-headquartered Uber and London-based Wayve are racing against the Google-owned Waymo and its Chinese equivalent Baidu’s Apollo Go to launch self-driving taxi services in London. Their progress is being watched closely because the British capital will be one of the first cities in the world to have American and Chinese tech firms operating on the same roads. Uber and Wayve said more than 100,000 Londoners were on their waiting list for the self-driving taxis. Transport for London (TfL), the capital’s licensing authority, granted 15 private hire vehicle licences to Ford Mustang Mach-E vehicles equipped with Wayve’s artificial intelligence driving software, as well as surround cameras and radar. The companies said TfL had confirmed they reached the required safety standards. A TfL-licensed private hire driver will sit in the driver’s seat during trips to intervene if necessary, although the software is expected to control the car.

The next step, of operating the taxis without a driver, will require Uber and Wayve to seek approval via a new process, known as an automated passenger services permit, with the government’s Driver and Vehicle Standards Agency. TfL said it would monitor the use of the vehicles, and was ready to intervene if passenger safety was compromised. A spokesperson said: “Safety is our top priority. Any new vehicle licensed to carry passengers on London’s roads must align with our Vision Zero goal of eliminating all deaths and serious injuries from collisions on London’s streets by 2041.” Wayve, which was co-founded by the New Zealand-born Alex Kendall , has been testing its tech in London since 2018 with safety drivers. In previous demonstrations to the Guardian the car has navigated most of the obstacles of north London’s busy roads, although the safety driver was forced to intervene at one point. Sarah Gates, Wayve’s vice-president for global affairs and assurance, said: “This licence is an important step towards giving Londoners the chance to experience autonomous driving technology. “The responsible deployment of these vehicles will bring us safer, cleaner and quieter streets, and we’re proud to continue working alongside regulators, communities and the public as we take the next steps towards making autonomous rides a reality in the capital.” View image in fullscreen Autonomous driving systems usually incorporate surround cameras and radar. Wayve also utilises AI. Photograph: The Lightwriter/Alamy The licence approval was not welcomed by minicab drivers, who fear the threat to their livelihood. Matthew Wright, a regional organiser for the GMB union, raised concerns about job losses, increased unemployment and liability for accidents, and said “extreme caution” was warranted from TfL.

Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Business Today Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion “This is a worrying development for our private hire driver members,” he said. “We can’t go charging ahead with new technologies without considering the implications of autonomous vehicles on all parties.” Driverless taxi services are already operating in several cities around the world, although mainly in the US and China, where most of the software developers are based. However, US companies are essentially blocked from China, and vice versa, meaning they have not had to compete directly. Uber abandoned its own efforts to develop self-driving technology in 2020, but it is working with several partners around the world who are in turn using different systems. That includes the Chinese company WeRide, which is operating driverless taxis in Abu Dhabi, UAE. Wayve is also working with the Japanese manufacturer Nissan on integrating its tech in private cars. The news came as Uber reported better than expected second-quarter gross bookings of $58. 02bn (£43bn), but said earnings for the next quarter would fall below Wall Street forecasts. The company also outlined ‌plans to spend more than $10bn on autonomous vehicles over the coming years, although it did not provide a specific ‌timeline.

articles.title: Ryan Murphy’s Teen Serial Killer Thriller The Shards Gets Stuck in the Shallow End

chapters.label: 【篇章1】

paras.en: Title: Ryan Murphy’s Teen Serial Killer Thriller The Shards Gets Stuck in the Shallow End
URL Source: https://time.com/article/2026/07/31/the-shards-review-fx/

Markdown Content:
A fruitful collaboration between [Ryan Murphy](https://time.com/5667752/ryan-murphy-netflix/) and Bret Easton Ellis sounds, at once, inevitable and impossible. Murphy is a maximalist in every sense—a superproducer pumping out [show](https://time.com/7372644/love-story-jfk-jr-carolyn-bessette-review/) after [operatic show](https://time.com/7355116/the-beauty-review-fx/), writing [characters](https://time.com/7331129/alls-fair-review/) who say the quiet part of every story out loud—and one of TV’s most influential promoters of [inclusive](https://time.com/5296664/ryan-murphy-pose/), [identity-politics-driven](https://time.com/5829141/hollywood-netflix-ryan-murphy-review/) programming. Ellis, for his part, is known for the minimalistic prose of his generation-defining debut novel, [_Less Than Zero_](https://time.com/archive/6703374/books-zombies-less-than-zero/), and a more recent culture-warrior phase in which he has inveighed against the same “[fake-woke corporate culture](https://www.interviewmagazine.com/culture/the-people-vs-bret-easton-ellis)” within the entertainment industry that some might say Murphy epitomizes. On the other hand, both men are inveterate provocateurs, unafraid to alienate audiences and fascinated by the psychology of psycho killers (see: Ellis’ [_American Psycho_](https://time.com/archive/6716218/books-a-revolting-development/)and a [huge chunk of Murphy’s output](https://time.com/7021155/american-sports-story-aaron-hernandez-ryan-murphy/)) and the interplay between pop culture and real life. Born on the boomer-Generation X cusp, they also remember what it was like to grow up gay in the ’80s.

In _The Shards_, which the two adapted from Ellis’ 2023 novel, the synergy among their experiences outweighs but doesn’t erase the irreconcilability of their perspectives. The story at its surface, an autofictional but otherwise familiar account of a serial killer stalking students at Ellis’ high school in 1981, gleams with the stylish production design, savvy genre pastiche, and elaborate set pieces for which Murphy is known. Yet it’s clear the show, premiering with two episodes on FX and Hulu on Aug. 5, has greater ambitions. In the connections it makes to cultural touchstones of its period and voiceover narration from a present-day Bret, _The Shards_ attempts to say something profound about the transition from youth to adulthood. Blame a mismatched creative team or the visual medium’s inherent privileging of images over ideas; the shallow stuff wins out.
![Image 1](https://static.time.com/v3/assets/bltea6093859af6183b/blt7ee6a4f4dca0f612/6a6cb2e21081ab5be99fbb3d/102_IMG_6043.jpeg?branch=production&width=3840&quality=75&auto=webp)
From left: Kaia Gerber, Igby Rigney, Hayes Warner, Homer Gere, and Graham Campbell in The Shards FX

Like _Less Than Zero_—and in some ways a prequel to that novel, which took place during a college break, though Bret (played by an unnervingly self-possessed Igby Rigney) is also writing the book while this story unfolds—_The Shards_ follows a clique of rich, debauched teens in L.A. Bret is noncommittally dating Debbie (rising pop star Hayes Warner), a ruthless go-getter, while secretly hooking up with guys. paras.en: Because so much of the meaning here resides in allusions that will elude most viewers under 40, Murphy and Ellis have essentially made two shows in one—an arch teen murder soap in the vein of [_Riverdale_](https://time.com/4649889/riverdale-cw-review/)-[_Pretty Little Liars_](https://time.com/4375361/shay-mitchell-pretty-little-liars-season-7/), and something more layered and harder to pin down for the older crowd. While the former benefits from the sensory intensity of Murphy’s storytelling (_The Shards_’ swimming pools achieve the incandescent blueness of [Donald Trump’s Reflecting Pool](https://time.com/article/2026/07/06/lincoln-memorial-reflecting-pool-repairs-Doug-Burgum-Algae-Gash/) dreams), and Ellis’ influence seems to have reined in some of his co-creator’s usual excesses, only the latter feels like something new. Yet the more thoughtful elements remain at the margins. It’s intriguing when the narrator says, for instance, “Matt had never felt about me the way I felt about him, which would be a recurring theme for the rest of my life.” The older Bret’s wistfulness, his frustration with a precocious teen Bret who traded his childhood innocence for an adult author’s life before he’d developed the self-knowledge that comes with genuine maturity, peeks through the surface without quite penetrating it.

_The Shards_ unravels in its final few episodes. One plays on the name of the crew’s hangout, Hamburger Hamlet, drawing Murphy-ish parallels between the characters and Shakespeare’s tragic personages that are so overwrought, they can’t be salvaged by self-awareness. The bigger disappointment is a bombshell ending, albeit a narratively ambiguous one, that fizzles rather than explodes. The psychological escalation that’s supposed to lead us there never fully happens. This show about the consequences of limited introspection suffers them as well.

articles.title: What to Say to Someone Who Is Dying, According to Hospice Workers

chapters.label: 【篇章1】

paras.en: Sydney Mishkin’s father had Stage IV sarcoma for seven years. In the weeks before he died, she kept trying to figure out what she still hadn’t told him. She searched through their old texts and listened to his voicemails. At night, she lay awake reviewing their entire relationship, desperate to identify the words she might one day regret leaving unsaid . Eventually, she realized there weren’t any. A week before her father passed away, Mishkin told him: “There’s nothing I’ve ever wanted to say and didn’t.” He was very weak, but he managed to answer: “I could not ask for a better daughter.” Within days, he was no longer able to speak. The exchange was deeply meaningful—but also bittersweet. Mishkin worried she had said too much or made her father feel obligated to summon the energy for a profound response. “How do you sum up a lifetime of loving somebody into a sentence or two?” she says. The answer, according to people who spend their careers alongside the dying, is that you don’t have to. There are words that can bring comfort, invite honesty, and help both of you find peace. But there’s no perfect script—and your presence likely matters more than anything you manage to say. When people ask Dr. Ira Byock whether they should make the trip to see a seriously ill friend or relative, he answers with a question: “Would you go to the funeral?” Almost always, they say yes—of course they would. "Well, go now,” says Byock, a palliative care physician in Montana and author of The Four Things That Matter Most . You'll say generous things at the memorial about what a remarkable person your friend was. Better to say them while she can hear you.

"It's much more fun to say those nice things when somebody is alive," Byock says. If you can only make one trip, make it this one. Hadley Vlahos, a hospice nurse and author of The In-Between: Unforgettable Encounters During Life's Final Moments , regularly hears from families who want her to alert them when the end is near. Her answer never changes. "You need to come right now," she says. "Everyone looks for this perfect time, and they always think that there's gonna be more time. " In hospice, the opposite is true: Beginning care earlier leaves more time for meaningful conversations. "You don't want to wait until they're in a coma," she says. The window for a real back-and-forth closes before most families expect it to. Start when the diagnosis arrives, says Dr. Kate Brazzale, chief medical officer of Empath Health , which operates Florida’s largest nonprofit hospice network. "Don't wait, because the person that's dying needs to be able to respond and speak," she says. "You need to get all those things out of the way. Towards the end, the person that's dying may not be able to speak, and it's not very fair to unload on them at that point. " Advertisement Sometimes there's no window at all. Christine Davies, director of spiritual care at Robert Wood Johnson University Hospital, has been a hospital chaplain for more than 25 years. She’s present for expected deaths after long illnesses, as well as sudden ones. "We may not even have the opportunity to say these last words, and so we have to say them all of the time," she says. paras.en: Advertisement The conversation can also turn toward the past. Davies uses an approach called life review, inviting people to reflect on the experiences that shaped a person’s life—the highs and lows, regrets and celebrations, important relationships, and the legacy they’ll leave. Put them in your own words if you like, but here’s how he phrases it: “Please forgive me. I forgive you. Thank you. I love you.” The first two are there because no relationship is perfect. "Within the history of almost all relationships, there are times of misunderstandings, hurt feelings, anger—sometimes real transgressions," Byock says. You can be specific about what you’re asking forgiveness for, or you can keep it general. “Dad, please forgive me, because I know I haven’t been the perfect son,” Byock offers as an example. “And I forgive you for the times that I felt misunderstood and harshly judged by you.” Advertisement In conversations between parents and children, Byock suggests adding an expression of pride. A parent might say, “I’m so proud to be your dad.” “Who else on the planet can tell your child how proud you are to be their mom or their dad?” he says. “That is a gift that keeps on giving.” A son or daughter can reverse it: “I’m so proud to be your daughter.” When the person dying is young, Byock focuses especially on this kind of affirmation. It’s a good conversation to have even if no one is sick.

Byock had it with his own mother in October 2003, prompted by the galleys of his book. They sat together, and he said nearly all of it, including thanking her for being his most steadfast supporter. There were tears, and they talked for an hour. A month later, his mother died suddenly of an undiagnosed heart condition. "I miss her," he says. "But there was nothing critically important left unsaid between my mom and me. " Advertisement Much of what frightens people at the end isn't about them. It's about everyone else. Vlahos sees it most clearly with the matriarch of a family—the woman who called all the kids every Sunday, who hosted every holiday. She describes a patient who seemed to be holding on, and whose sons finally said the thing she needed to hear to pass peacefully: “I promise I'm still going to call Dad every Sunday. I promise we're still going to have Christmas.” Vlahos remembers a patient who was told, “I promise to make sure your grandson knows you.” "I think that matters a lot more than people think," she says. Then there are the reassurances almost no one thinks to offer. Brazzale says patients who are declining may worry about soiling themselves, losing their dignity, or being moved out of their home at the end. What she’d want to hear, she says, is this: “We’re going to keep you clean. We’re going to keep you safe. We’re going to keep you comfortable.” If dying at home is the plan, family can add: “We’re going to keep you home.” “There’s something about cleanliness that resonates with people,” she says. “It sounds simple, but it’s quite powerful.”

Advertisement In the final phase of dying—a period Barbara Karnes, a hospice nurse and educator since the 1970s, calls labor—many people become nonresponsive. “What we watchers can do is talk as if they can hear us,” she says. Hearing is thought to be one of the last senses to fade, so continue as though your loved one may still hear you. Brazzale offers similar advice: If you run out of things to say, choose a beautiful book and read aloud. paras.en: She has watched families push patients through a 10th round of chemotherapy so no one can say they gave up. "There's going to be a point at which they die, and you should never frame it that they gave up," she says. "What a terrible thing, that 100% of the human race is just going to quit. " Advertisement Platitudes often spring from the urge to talk someone out of what they’re feeling. But if a dying person says, “This sucks,” you don’t need to insist otherwise. “You can be like, ‘Yeah, you know what, it does,’” Vlahos says. Making room for that honesty also helps relieve the dying person of another burden: managing everyone else’s emotions. Loved ones rarely mean to put them in that position, Vlahos says, but she sees it happen often. That means silence is a legitimate option. Vlahos believes many of these important final encounters don’t happen because people feel pressure to find the right words. “Sometimes the right thing to say is nothing—to just let someone talk,” she says. Davies gives her chaplaincy students a five-word rule: “Show up and shut up.” Her interns sometimes come to her surprised that a grieving family hugged them, because they felt they hadn’t done anything. “No—you bore witness to what they were going through,” she tells them. “‘You were there in the hardest moment, and you didn’t fill it with words. You allowed for the silence to take place.’ We try not to cheer people up, because there’s no cheering up.” Advertisement You don’t have to hold yourself together, either. Vlahos would far rather someone show up and cry with her than stay away. Brazzale once made the same point, half-jokingly, to her own children.

She initially told them she didn’t want anyone crying at her bedside when she died—then reconsidered. “Actually, you’d better shed a few tears,” she told them. “Because that shows I mattered.” The person who is dying is grieving, too, Brazzale says. Trying to protect each other by hiding that sadness can create distance at a moment when time together is especially precious. “Don’t be tiptoeing around one another for fear of hurting each other’s feelings,” she says, “because the scars left behind will be that much deeper.”

Vlahos would far rather someone show up and cry with her than stay away. Brazzale once made the same point, half-jokingly, to her own children.

She initially told them she didn’t want anyone crying at her bedside when she died—then reconsidered. “Actually, you’d better shed a few tears,” she told them. “Because that shows I mattered.” The person who is dying is grieving, too, Brazzale says. Trying to protect each other by hiding that sadness can create distance at a moment when time together is especially precious. “Don’t be tiptoeing around one another for fear of hurting each other’s feelings,” she says, “because the scars left behind will be that much deeper.”

paras.en: Title: Europeans Are Considering Placing This American-Born Singer on a New Banknote
URL Source: https://time.com/article/2026/08/04/new-euro-banknotes-american-greek-maria-callas-culture-redesign/

Markdown Content:
The European Central Bank (ECB) is [redesigning its euro banknotes](https://www.ecb.europa.eu/euro/banknotes/future_banknotes/html/index.en.html#resources) and the public is playing a key role in deciding how the new bills will look.
Two core redesign proposals are being considered—with each offering a different interpretation of its theme across the €5, €10, €20, €50, €100, and €200 bills.

One redesign package focuses on European culture, with banknotes set to feature faces of prominent talents, including American-born singer Maria Callas. The other is centered on nature, featuring imagery of rivers and birds.

Europeans have been invited to give their views on the final selection through an online survey which closes Sept. 21. The results will be considered by the Governing Council of the ECB, along with independent jury conclusions and a technical review, before the final design is selected toward the end of 2026.
The new banknotes would then undergo testing before entering circulation, while remaining interchangeable with the current series of euro notes.

According to the ECB, the redesign [aims](https://www.ecb.europa.eu/euro/banknotes/future_banknotes/html/index.en.html#survey) to better reflect Europe's identity and values, introduce enhanced security features, improve environmental sustainability, and make the banknotes more accessible and easier to use.

As it’s the first major redesign of the euro banknotes since the currency notes were [introduced](https://european-union.europa.eu/institutions-law-budget/euro/history-and-purpose_en) in 2002, the stakes are high.

“Talk to friends, colleagues, family members, and ask them to participate, because we want as many Europeans as possible to express their views about our future banknotes,” [said](https://x.com/Lagarde/status/2082390939801382979) ECB president Christine Lagarde.

As for the choices at hand, the rivers and birds series highlights wildlife found across Europe. The designs spotlight species including the wallcreeper, kingfisher, bee-eater, white stork, avocet, and northern gannet against a range of serene landscapes.
Meanwhile, there are some very recognizable faces of people credited with shaping the continent’s cultural identity in the European culture redesign package.

German symphonist Ludwig van Beethoven, considered one of the greatest composers of the 18th and 19th centuries; Polish-French scientist Marie Curie, known for discovering radium and polonium;Spanish author Miguel de Cervantes, who wrote _Don Quixote_; Italian polymath Leonardo da Vinci, famed for painting the _Mona Lisa_; and Austrian novelist and peace activist Bertha von Suttner, the first woman to receive the [Nobel Peace Prize](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/peace/1905/suttner/facts/).
American-Greek soprano Callas is set to appear on the new €5 banknote, should the cultural package be selected.
![Image 1](https://static.time.com/v3/assets/bltea6093859af6183b/blt1de4b3e048e0dd19/6a733494d6cd0e134984c083/CallasCover.png?branch=production&width=2400&quality=75&auto=webp)
The Oct. 29, 1956, cover of TIME HENRY KOERNER

While the other figures featured in the proposed designs were born in Europe, Callas was [born](https://www.maria-callas.com/cms/files/file/mariacallas-thefullstory-en.pdf) in New York in December 1923 to Greek parents.
Often hailed as one of the greatest sopranos of the 20th century, she moved to Athens with her mother as a teenager.

Callas was a pupil of the celebrated Spanish soprano [Elvira de Hidalgo](https://adp.library.ucsb.edu/index.php/mastertalent/detail/311314/Hidalgo_Elvira_de) at the Athens Conservatory. Her own career went on to span decades across many of the world's leading opera houses.

In 1951 she made her official debut at La Scala in Milan, performing Verdi's _I Vespri Siciliani_. From there, she appeared on some of the world's most prestigious stages, including the Royal Opera House in London, the Metropolitan Opera in New York, and the Paris Opera.

The English National Opera [describes](https://www.eno.org/discover-opera/articles/the-beginners-guide-to-maria-callas/) her as being “able to deliver a wide range of vocal colours depending on the mood or type of music she was singing.”

According to her [biography](https://mariacallasmuseum.gr/en/about-the-divina/) at the Maria Callas Museum in Athens, Callas “is widely recognized as the foremost Opera icon of the 20th century, renowned for her unmatched interpretations and techniques.”
When TIME put Callas on the cover of the Oct. 29, 1956, issue, the magazine dubbed her “the undisputed queen of the world’s opera.”

Callas made her final major recital appearance in Sapporo, Japan in 1974, and withdrew from public life to live in Paris, where she [died of a heart attack](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/03/06/arts/music/maria-callas-dead.html) in 1977, at the age of 53.
Across the world, Callas' legacy continues to be recognized.

Greece's Ministry of Culture successfully [organized](https://www.culture.gov.gr/el/Information/SitePages/view.aspx?nID=4427) for the centenary of her birth to be included in UNESCO's 2023 anniversary commemorations.

articles.title: AI models shock UK testers by using stolen identities to trick developers

chapters.label: 【篇章1】

paras.en: AISI said the rogue behaviour was carried out by agents powered by two models – Anthropic’s Mythos 5 and OpenAI’s GPT-5. 6 Sol. Photograph: Dado Ruvić/Reuters View image in fullscreen AISI said the rogue behaviour was carried out by agents powered by two models – Anthropic’s Mythos 5 and OpenAI’s GPT-5. 6 Sol. Photograph: Dado Ruvić/Reuters AI (artificial intelligence) AI models shock UK testers by using stolen identities to trick developers AI Security Institute says models by OpenAI and Anthropic went rogue during a cybersecurity test and showed a new type of risk Prefer the Guardian on Google Advanced AI models developed by OpenAI and Anthropic went rogue during a cybersecurity test and showed a new type of risk posed by the technology, according to the UK’s AI Security Institute. AISI described the actions carried out by the agents – the term for AI systems that can perform tasks without human help – as a “serious incident”. In one example, an agent powered by Anthropic’s Mythos model sent targeted emails to people. AISI said the rogue behaviour was carried out by agents powered by two models – Anthropic’s Mythos 5 and OpenAI’s GPT-5. 6 Sol. AISI said it detected unusual activity during a routine cybersecurity test for AI models on 28 July. It found that some of the agents had engaged in “sustained, potentially harmful activity directed at real people and organisations”. It took an hour to contain the incident. In the most serious case, an agent powered by Mythos tried to insert malicious code into an open-source software project on GitHub, a platform used by software developers. In an attempt to get the code approved, the agent then created fake online identities based on real people and used them to press the project’s overseer into accepting the code.

These attempts were blocked by a human developer. AISI said the agent used techniques commonly associated with real-world hackers. It sent emails to specifically chosen individuals – a technique known as “spear-phishing” – that attempted to manipulate the recipient. Some of the messages contained harmful software. AISI said no harm was caused but the agents’ actions were unprecedented. “This is the first time we have seen risks around autonomy and deception manifest this clearly, without specific prompting, in the real world,” said AISI in a blogpost . The incident followed recent similar episodes at OpenAI and Anthropic. In July, OpenAI said an agent powered by its models had hacked an AI startup during a test, and days later Anthropic said its Claude model had hacked three organisations during an evaluation. AISI said the incident, taken alongside similar occurrences at OpenAI and Anthropic, represented a “shift in the risk landscape”. This was not an example of deliberate misuse of publicly available models, AISI said, but showed models in a research environment taking unintended action “beyond their authorised scope”. AISI said 17 of the 19 cases of rogue behaviour that occurred during the evaluation were carried out by Mythos and two by Sol. AISI said this was not a case of a model escaping its “sandbox”, or secure testing environment. The institute said it had intentionally permitted internet access and disabled filters within the models that blocked dangerous behaviour. The models are not publicly available in those operating conditions and there is no sign of such behaviour happening outside tests, AISI said.

Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Business Today Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion The incident should be interpreted with “caution and nuance”, AISI said, but the signs of deceptive behaviour were “to an extent and severity we did not anticipate”. It was a small number of events that occurred under specific conditions, AISI added, but it had not happened before. “What we can say is that the behaviour was possible, sustained and new. That alone warrants attention,” AISI said. AISI admitted it was not actively monitoring the agents’ behaviour during the evaluation. It said it was putting tighter controls on internet access in tests as a result of the incident, introducing constant monitoring of tests and reassessing its design of tests. It said evaluations should assume a model would attempt to act beyond its remit. The UK’s AI minister, Kanishka Narayan, said it was “absolutely vital” that the UK had a world-leading AI safety organisation. “Identifying new behaviour like this and sharing our findings, so we can tackle it, is exactly what AISI was set up to do,” he said. OpenAI said the testing occurred during “conditions that do not reflect ordinary use”. An OpenAI spokesperson said: “We’ll continue working with evaluators and other stakeholders across the industry to strengthen shared practices for conducting evaluations safely as models become more capable.” Anthropic said the incident “underscores the need for a broader conversation about how to safely evaluate increasingly capable AI agents” and it would continue to work with AISI on evaluating what happened.

paras.en: Science Weekly Science Four types of thinker, the cyclosporiasis outbreak, and the UK’s biggest telescope threatened – podcast Madeleine Finlay is joined by Ian Sample, Guardian science editor, to discuss three eye-catching science stories including an investigation that has identified four distinct types of thinker. Also on the agenda is the unprecedented cyclosporiasis outbreak in the US which has now been linked to two fatalities, and the funding cuts that threaten the iconic Jodrell Bank world heritage site, home to the Lovell telescope More ways to listen Apple podcasts Spotify RSS Feed Download Presented by Madeleine Finlay , with Ian Sample , produced by Ellie Sans and Madeleine Finlay , sound design by Joel Cox , the executive producer was Ellie Bury Thu 6 Aug 2026 05.00 BST Share Clip: CSPAN Four types of thinker have been identified. Which one are you? CDC reportedly expands scope of US cyclosporiasis outbreak to 15 states Artists, writers and scientists urge UK government to save Jodrell Bank Observatory Support the Guardian: theguardian.com/sciencepod

articles.title: One Night Only’s Preposterous Premise Gives Way to a Delightful Romantic Comedy

chapters.label: 【篇章1】

paras.en: Barbaro and Turner during one of their many run-ins in One Night Only —Courtesy of Universal

Either you’ve seen the statistics or you’re living them: 
Millennials
 and members of Gen Z are 
having less sex
 than previous generations did. The reasons aren’t exactly clear—economic insecurity, coupled with after-effects of the pandemic, may have something to do with it—but anecdotally, at least, the trend is real. What if, God forbid, a fascist government decreed that unmarried people could have sex on just one night of the year? Would that shift anything in the way young people think about coupling, for a night or a lifetime? And would it make them long for freedom they can’t have?

Those are some of the questions posed by Will Gluck’s preposterous and delightful romantic comedy 
One Night Only, 
set in a dystopian present where the government controls when and how unmarried people can have sex: It has to be on one designated night of the year, and using protection is a requirement. The nuts and bolts of the premise don’t matter much: presumably, this fictitious government thinks it’s promoting so-called family values, though its more nefarious aim may be to deprive its citizens of freedom and joy. The point is that on just one night a year, all the singles go crazy. The women put on their tiniest, sparkliest dresses and highest heels and head out, looking for romance or at least just a tumble. Then men spruce up a bit too, or at least put on a clean shirt, and though some have honorable intentions, there are others who maintain strict schedules so they can pack multiple conquests into a night. Men will be men—or at least some of them will be.
The romance of pizza in One Night Only —Courtesy of Universal

As you can imagine, this specified “one night” would be especially mad in a city like New York, where people are often a little nuts to begin with, and that’s where 
One Night Only 
takes place. Owen (
Callum Turner
, rendering a reasonably believable American accent) runs a pizza joint, and he’s getting ready to close up shop as this special 12-hour night is set to begin. He’s not married, but he does have a girlfriend (played by 
Maya Hawke
), who informs him, when they meet up for their date, that she wants to use this one free night of premarital sex to sleep with someone else. Owen is crestfallen. But he also figures he may as well try his own luck. That’s how he runs into Allie (
Monica Barbaro
), also on her own. She’s had a tough workday—she’s a singer, and she’s been toiling in the studio, recording a schmaltzy jingle for a psoriasis commercial—and her evening plans have fallen through: the pal she was set to go out with, Jacinta (King Princess), found herself a literal prince in the early hours of the evening and has taken off. Allie’s roommate (Quintessa Swindell), who happens to be gay and has no interest in these one-night-only shenanigans (“We’ve been dancing around your laws since before the Bible,” they explain, suggesting that the city’s gay population has pretty much ignored the premarital-sex ban altogether), urges her to make the most of the evening, kitting her out in a fetching, if minuscule, green sequined dress left behind by an ex-girlfriend. In this splendid and very hot outfit, completed with spindly heeled sandals, Allie reluctantly toddles off into the night to join her glimmering, mini-skirted sisters. On this night, New York has become a city of stems.

Allie and Owen run into each other early on, and the sparks fly, but only until Owen—who downed two quick kamikazes in the wake of his girlfriend’s announcement—nearly barfs all over Allie’s dainty shoes. She’s disgusted. They part ways, only to be serendipitously reunited several times as the evening progresses. After being propositioned by one loser after another in a swanky bar, Allie meets a gorgeous charmer (Andrew Burnap) whose apartment is decked out with an original 
Banksy
, and maybe a Basquiat; Owen swipes right on a cutie who lures him from somewhere in Manhattan to Brooklyn Bridge Park—he jumps on a CitiBike and pedals like crazy to get there. Both of these assignations fall through, and somehow, Allie and Owen keep finding themselves thrown together. Their loathing for one another grows. They jab at one another endlessly. You can see where this is headed.
Obtaining contraception requires Herculean effort —Courtesy of Universal

The script, by Travis Braun, makes the most of the story’s intentionally absurd premise. As you can imagine, condoms are a hot commodity on this magical night: in one scene, the city’s last remaining prophylactic becomes an object akin to Indiana Jones’ Ark of the Covenant. Housed in its own Plexiglass pyramid and guarded by two golden mannequins, it serves as the glowing center of one of the movie’s goofiest sight gags. And Gluck, whose last film was the 2023 Glen Powell-Sidney Sweeney vehicle

,
 has the benefit of two appealing co-stars here. The movie knows that Owen, although a decent guy—and certainly hot, in that show-offy, gym-guy way—is a bit of a goober: Turner goes along with that idea amiably, and even the rather boring polo shirt he’s wearing—which becomes fodder for one of the movie’s great punchlines—is such a stark contrast to Allie’s glittering stunner of a dress that you almost believe he’s not good enough for her. Really, he’s perfectly OK. The problem may be that Allie, as Barbaro plays her, is off-the-charts enchanting. Barbaro—who was superb as Joan Baez in James Mangold’s 2024 Bob Dylan movie

—knows how to land a zinger and make it feel like a kiss blown from across the room. With her shy, slow-burning smile, she carries echoes of 
Natalie Wood
. When the movie threatens to sag, she’s the one holding it aloft.

chapters.label: 【篇章2】

paras.en:
But she’s not the only unassuming superstar in 
One Night Only. This is a great New York movie, one that captures all the beauty and dumb grit of this fantastic, weird city. On this night of all nights, the youngsters at play aren’t just piling into Ubers like spoiled rich kids. They’re actually riding the subway, as broke young people continue to do, and the stations look to have been only just slightly spruced up for their big closeups—you won’t see any Pizza Rats, but you might notice a stray gum wrapper here or there. The movie also makes great use of some the city's underrepresented landmarks, like Washington Heights' adorable Little Red Lighthouse, made famous by Hildegarde Swift’s 1947 children’s book 
The Little Red Lighthouse and the Great Gray Bridge. It all seems too good to be true—but it isn't. One Night Only
 gives us a New York that’s only a semi-fantasy, a place where, even in the face of encroaching corporate chains, you can still see small, independently owned restaurants announcing their presence with the warmth of a neon sign. It’s true that, in real life, these spots are disappearing. But so many of them hang on, in a city that, against all odds, continues to hang on to everything human and real and perhaps just a bit crazy. One Night Only
 still believes in the glorious unpredictability of New York, just as it believes in love and freedom and the joy and messiness of amorous adventures. It’s a movie extolling the pleasures of sex and the city, in that order.

articles.title: Sesame Street Has A New Extreme Weather Episode. Here's What Climate Experts Think

chapters.label: 【篇章1】

paras.en: It’s been a summer of climate extremes—from record-breaking heat waves to deadly flash floods to a fire season that has seen a number of acres burned well above the 10-year average. Even Sesame Street , where sunny days once swept the clouds away, can’t seem to keep the storms at bay. A new special, Storm on Sesame Street , which aired on Aug. 3, follows Elmo and friends as they work together to get ready for a big storm, and help rebuild in its aftermath. The episode was created to help kids better understand extreme weather as it becomes increasingly more frequent. “Extreme weather is now a reality for many families, and young children need support they can understand and trust,” Joseph Giraldi, chief operating officer of Sesame Workshop, said in a press release. “With our Extreme Weather response initiative, we’re using the power of Sesame Street to help children prepare for what’s ahead, cope with big emotions during moments of disruption, and begin to recover afterward. From our new storm special to year‑round resources and community outreach, this initiative reflects our commitment to showing up for children and families when they need it most.” The episode provides an opening for adults to help prepare kids about what to expect during an extreme weather event—before it actually happens. Elmo and his father help hand out food and water to their neighbors, talk through the big emotions the storm brings up, and find ways to help their friends when the storm leaves Sesame Street unrecognizable. “It's really important, and I think it can fall off a lot of our radars to have emergency plans or to know what should be in an emergency kit,” says Samantha Harrington, director of audience experience for Yale Climate Connections.

“People don't always make great decisions when they're in an emergency situation, or when they're stressed. So as much as you can make that decision-making earlier before the emergency happens, then you're going to be a lot better prepared to react and respond in a way that is going to be the safest and calmest for you and your child.” Sesame Street first tackled extreme weather in the episode, Sesame Street Gets Through a Storm , which premiered in 2001 and featured Big Bird rebuilding his nest after it was destroyed in a hurricane. The episode re-aired in the aftermath of Hurricane Katrina and Hurricane Sandy. In the years since, extreme weather events, fueled in no small part by climate change, have become hard for most Americans to ignore. There has been a “staggering rise” in climate-related disasters in the 21st century, according to the United Nations . Nearly one in five Americans have had to evacuate their homes due to extreme weather conditions, according to an October 2024 poll conducted by YouGov . Children born in 2020 are projected to experience up to seven times more extreme weather events than those born in 1960. Advertisement Sesame Street plans to provide resources to help families, including a printed and digital storybook, to help children heal when the things they love are lost, articles and activities that support children and families as they deal with environmental stressors like heat or air quality, and plans to distribute “go bags” with essentials to support families during evacuations and periods of displacement. It’s an important first step in getting children and families more equipped for dealing with extreme weather events—which most Americans are woefully underprepared for.

In one 2025 survey of 2,000 adults by Talker Research , 90% said it's critical to be prepared for extreme weather, but only 46% had an emergency plan in place. The episode opens the channel of communication in an age appropriate way, experts say. “It's covering all of the bases,” says Adam Rainear, associate professor of communication and media at West Chester University, whose work focuses on climate communications. “It's giving the messaging so that kids are aware and alert, but also not making them afraid of everything around them.” While Elmo and his friend Abby acknowledge their fear, they focus on having courage—and when Elmo’s courage falters as the power goes out, his dad steps in to help with words of encouragement and an exercise to help calm him down. Advertisement Tina Grotzer, principal research scientist at Harvard University, who works at the intersection of climate change and education, hopes that any future episodes on the topic can be more explicit in drawing the connection between extreme weather and climate change, which is not mentioned in the episode. “This is a generation of kids for whom extreme weather is becoming more and more common, and they have to somehow walk this balance of normalizing kids' experiences, but also helping kids to know that this is only the new normal in terms of recent times,” she says. “It may seem subtle, but if we talk about people all around the world engaging in actions, a lot of people together can make a difference. We can't change the weather we're getting today, but over time we can do things to care for Earth.”

We can't change the weather we're getting today, but over time we can do things to care for Earth.”

articles.title: By day five of my labour, I didn’t want an ‘ideal birth’. I only wanted to survive | Natalie Morris

chapters.label: 【篇章1】

paras.en: Illustration: PA/Alamy/Getty/Guardian Design View image in fullscreen Illustration: PA/Alamy/Getty/Guardian Design Opinion Women's health By day five of my labour, I didn’t want an ‘ideal birth’. I only wanted to survive Natalie Morris Yvette Cooper’s maternity reforms must change a system that too often fails women when they’re at their most vulnerable O n the third day of being in labour with my first child, I entered a new state of being. It was time to dig deep. This is what I had learned in all the childbirth classes. As long as I remained calm, breathed as instructed, moaned through the pain, things would happen as they were meant to. My body knew what it was doing. Only, it didn’t. On the fourth day, I started to beg. This wasn’t right. Despite contraction after relentless contraction, I wasn’t dilating. I hadn’t slept, I couldn’t even sit down. I needed help. And still, they waited. For what, I never understood. When Yvette Cooper told the Guardian this week that women must not “feel pressurised” to have “an ideal birth experience”, it was a relief to hear her name this all-too-common phenomenon in which maternity staff are reluctant – or refusing – to escalate. But Cooper’s characterisation of the problem is not the full picture. The harm here is not just in women being nudged towards a certain kind of birth experience, but in a culture that can completely override women’s physical and psychological safety in favour of a low-intervention ideal. Half of Britain’s maternal deaths are considered preventable , and low-intervention births are the ideal for a reason. Midwife-led care usually results in better outcomes for healthy women with straightforward pregnancies – lower risk of infection and severe bleeds, and quicker recovery.

In 2024-25, 45% of all hospital deliveries in England (542,235 total births) were performed via caesarean section – it was the first time C-sections outnumbered unassisted natural vaginal births. (Another 11% needed extra support through instruments such as forceps.) There is a natural, and warranted, cautiousness about the over-medicalisation of birth, which can lead to avoidable complications, and leave women who would prefer a natural birth feeling pressured to take a different route. But we can’t ignore that there are also structural forces at play here: lower intervention also translates to lower cost for an overstretched, under-resourced system. One midwife told me explicitly that they would have admitted me to the labour ward earlier if there had been a bed. Of course most first-time mothers would choose the lowest possible intervention if they could. I had hoped to float blissfully in a birthing pool under the soft glow of fairy lights. But when it comes to the messy, unpredictable, dangerous act of bringing new life into the world, the concept of choice can quickly be revealed as a fallacy. By day five of my labour, I was not thinking about my birth plan. I was not thinking about very much at all. My only focus was survival. The demographic of people giving birth today looks nothing like it did 30 years ago. The average age of a mother in England and Wales is now 31 , a figure that has been creeping up since records began. There is something deeply flawed about a system that pushes quite so strongly for low-intervention births despite the fact that mothers over 30 are more likely to require a higher level of medical involvement.

Almost half of UK women aged 30-39 have caesareans, and for those over 40, it is now the most common way to give birth. Yet the narrative of an “ideal birth” persists, leaving women who end up needing more help wondering where they went wrong. Maternity practices must reflect this reality, or risk perpetuating a cycle that leaves women at risk and then pushes the blame back on to them. After the best part of a week, I was eventually wheeled down for an emergency C-section. Even then, it wasn’t the desperate pleas from my husband and me that finally spurred action, it was the fact that my baby started showing signs of distress. The doctors who greeted us displayed clear consternation that I had been left in that state for so long, a factor that probably played a part in my child developing an irregular heartbeat. The ideal birth narrative – that low-intervention, midwife-led care is always best – has hardened into institutional bias, amid a system in which women’s choices about their medical care are too often sidelined. In one of her first acts as health secretary, Cooper said she intends to reintroduce binding national maternity standards. They will include ending the postcode lottery for levels of care, and tackling racial inequalities that have meant worse outcomes for poorer and for black and Asian women. Her promises sound reassuring, but we have heard similar things before. What’s needed is a fundamental cultural shift so that women’s voices are treated as clinical evidence, not background noise. There is a deep-rooted disconnect in NHS maternity units. Between the needs of patients and the people treating them, and between different parts of the system itself.

chapters.label: 【篇章2】

paras.en: When midwife-led care and obstetric intervention are positioned in opposition, rather than as complementary approaches, escalation can be perceived as failure instead of necessary care. And in that gap, women at their most vulnerable have their pain minimised and their instincts questioned, sometimes to the point that risk becomes life-threatening. For me and thousands of other mothers, our births could have gone so differently if we had only been heard. My ideal birth is not defined by candlelight or calm breathing. It is one where I am listened to, believed and responded to in time. One that both my baby and I survive at any cost. Natalie Morris is the author of Mixed/Other: Explorations of Multiraciality in Modern Britain Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? articles.title: ‘James Dean has got nothing on that kid’: River Phoenix films – ranked!

chapters.label: 【篇章1】

paras.en: River Phoenix as young Indiana Jones in Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade (1989) . Photograph: Landmark Media/Alamy View image in fullscreen River Phoenix as young Indiana Jones in Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade (1989) . Photograph: Landmark Media/Alamy Ranked Film ‘James Dean has got nothing on that kid’: River Phoenix films – ranked! As Stand By Me is re-released for its 40th anniversary, we look at the late actor’s most intense, enduring roles – from a goofball boffin to a narcoleptic hustler Prefer the Guardian on Google 16. Circle of Violence: A Family Drama (1986) Issue-of-the-week TV movie about elder abuse, with Tuesday Weld as a harried mum taking out her frustrations on her own ageing mother. Phoenix slaps on the hair gel as the essentially decent son who blasts his music too loud, lets his rowdy if unusually spiffy pals put their feet on the furniture and resents the new house guest: “Grandma is really getting on my nerves!” View image in fullscreen ‘Mad with grief’ … Phoenix in Silent Tongue. Photograph: United Archives GmbH/Alamy Sam Shepard’s turgid western premiered at Sundance in early 1993, then sat on the shelf for a year. As with his unfinished final film, Dark Blood, Phoenix plays a desert-dwelling widower gone mad with grief. In this case, his father (Richard Harris) steals a second wife for him from the travelling showman (Alan Bates) who sold him his first. Nuance is not required from Phoenix here, just doleful, brooding twitchiness. A family connection: his brother Joaquin later played Harris’s son, too, in Gladiator. Directed by Peter Bogdanovich, this was the last film Phoenix completed.

Samantha Mathis (his then girlfriend), Dermot Mulroney and a pre-fame Sandra Bullock are aspiring country-and-western musicians convening in Nashville, but their warm, lively work only underlines how ill at ease Phoenix seems on screen. As the most gifted performer of the bunch, he is remote in ways that can’t easily be explained away as acting choices. “He looks ill,” observed the critic Roger Ebert, who thought the performance “should have been seen by someone as a cry for help”. View image in fullscreen Son of a sleeper agent … Phoenix in Little Nikita. Photograph: Cine Text/Sportsphoto/Allstar Espionage for dummies. Phoenix is the all-American high-schooler Jeff, who has no inkling that he is really Nikita, son of Russian sleeper agents. That’s until undercover FBI man Sidney Poitier cosies up to him and spills the beans. Both deserve better than this minefield of spy-movie cliches, but you’ll never catch Phoenix coasting. He delivers the line “Truth has no meaning in this house!” with all the conviction of James Dean in Rebel Without a Cause screaming, “You’re tearing me apart!” Despite a strong cast (Ellen Burstyn, Molly Ringwald, Paul Sorvino) and direction by British television veteran Waris Hussein (Doctor Who, Henry VIII and His Six Wives), this TV movie about a teen suicide pact is mostly soapy and simplistic. Phoenix is affectingly uninhibited, though, as the grieving sibling: “Boy, he must have hated us,” he weeps after the death of his beloved older brother. He won a Young Artist award for his troubles, beating his co-star, Poltergeist poppet Heather O’Rourke, who died three years later at the age of 12. View image in fullscreen On-set tensions … Phoenix with Judy Davis and Jonathan Pryce in Dark Blood. Photograph: TCD/Prod.

DB/Alamy A little more than half of Phoenix’s final movie was in the can when he died of a drug overdose on 31 October 1993. Director George Sluizer stole the footage to prevent it being destroyed, then used stills and narration to plug the gaps in a patchwork cut which premiered in 2012, two years before his own death. Phoenix plays a widowed recluse who rescues a married couple (Jonathan Pryce and Judy Davis) after their Bentley breaks down near his desert shack; Knife in the Water-style thriller dynamics ensue. Phoenix is a haunted, enigmatic presence but only Davis’s performance truly coheres. On-set tensions were rife between her and Sluizer; he accused her of giving Phoenix hell, though producer Stephen Woolley recalls the young actor kissing Davis’s feet. Broad, wacky comedy about a wronged wife (Tracey Ullman) plotting to murder her philandering husband (Kevin Kline, whose performance in A Fish Called Wanda beat Phoenix to the best supporting actor Oscar in 1989). She is encouraged and assisted by, variously, her own mother (Joan Plowright), who sets the plan in motion; an earnest hippy (Phoenix), whom the couple employ at their pizza joint, and who has his own reasons for wanting the husband out of the way; and a pair of stoned amateur hit-men (William Hurt and Keanu Reeves). Phoenix denied that his character, with his crystals, beads and mysticism, bore any resemblance to himself (“Nope, no similarities whatsoever”) but he feels at the very least like a riff on the actor’s persona. View image in fullscreen Code-breaking caper … Phoenix in Sneakers. Photograph: Universal/Allstar According to Esquire magazine, Phoenix was embarrassed by the commercialism of this engaging code-breaking caper, and even advised his friends not to watch it.
