paras.en: Admittedly, there isn’t a whole lot for him to do on screen, but at least he and Poitier, previously paired in Little Nikita, get to participate in a superior espionage adventure this time around. They’re part of the eccentric tech-security team headed by Robert Redford (who had just picked Brad Pitt for the lead role coveted by Phoenix in the fly-fishing drama A River Runs Through It). The rest of Redford’s crew includes David Strathairn and Dan Aykroyd, who in one scene is wearing a T-shirt advertising Aleka’s Attic, the jangly folk-pop outfit fronted by Phoenix. View image in fullscreen With Matthew Perry in A Night in the Life of Jimmy Reardon. Photograph: 20 Century Fox/Allstar Phoenix was a reluctant heartthrob, so it follows that his one bona fide teen movie would be unorthodox and melancholy. As Jimmy, a slick, priapic but troubled young poet whose sexual partners include one of his mother’s friends, Phoenix flirts with the dislikable and unsympathetic. In one scene, he loses interest during his girlfriend’s elaborate masked-intruder sex fantasy: “I don’t feel like Jack the Ripper today.” In another, he is scolded by his best pal (a pre-Friends Matthew Perry), who tells him: “Your goddam pecker leads you around like a mule chasing a carrot.” Twentieth Century Fox re-edited the movie as a splashy comedy; director William Richert’s cut, retitled Aren’t You Even Gonna Kiss Me Goodbye? after his original novel, is the classier version. He and Phoenix were reunited when Richert played the Falstaffian vagabond Bob in My Own Private Idaho. Richert died in 2022; his website still advertises a crowd-funding campaign to pay for “deepface [sic] technology” that would insert Phoenix into the director’s version of The Man with the Iron Mask.

The most delirious part of this threequel is its breakneck, origin-story prologue, with Phoenix (who was recommended for the role by his Mosquito Coast co-star Harrison Ford) showing how the young Indiana Jones acquired his bullwhip, battered fedora, chin scar and ophidiophobia. It’s such a hoot that only a spoilsport would ask why a strictly-parented Boy Scout in 1912 Utah sports the unruly surfer-dude fringe of a 1980s teen idol. Joe Dante used his Gremlins clout to make this charming goofball fantasy starring Phoenix and Ethan Hawke, both 14, as friends who build and pilot a rinky-dink spaceship. Making his movie debut after several years of TV work, Phoenix was already on course to be a teen pin-up but was cast against type as the boffin Wolfgang. Hawke recalls seeing his co-star for the first time walking back and forth outside their motel: “[I] asked him what he was doing, and he said he was trying to figure out how Wolfgang walked … from that moment forward he was always ahead of me.” Next to him, said Hawke, “I never felt more ordinary in my life.” View image in fullscreen With Harrison Ford, Helen Mirren and Hilary Gordon in Mosquito Coast. Photograph: Cinetext Collection/Sportsphoto/Allstar Peter Weir’s dogged, Paul Schrader-scripted adaptation of Paul Theroux’s novel about a ranting, idealistic inventor who drags his family off to live in the Central American rainforests is dominated by Harrison Ford’s oppressive performance. The rest of the cast, including Helen Mirren as his wife, scarcely get a look-in, though Phoenix makes a strong impression as the adoring eldest son whose idolatry gives way to mounting horror at his father’s murderous insanity.

Phoenix’s then-girlfriend, Martha Plimpton, has a memorable scene in which she speaks for his thousands of teenage fans by admitting: “I think of you when I go to the bathroom.” Hot from his Oscar nomination for Running on Empty, Phoenix was granted director approval for this drama about a group of callous young Marines competing in a “dogfight” to find the ugliest date during their last night before being shipped off to Okinawa, and then to Vietnam. He wisely chose the film-maker Nancy Savoca, who brings a complex tenderness to the emotional tussles between Eddie (Phoenix) and his prey, the shy waitress and amateur balladeer Rose (Lili Taylor), who turns out to be nobody’s fool. Phoenix doesn’t soft-pedal Eddie’s cruelty, which makes his pangs of conscience even more resonant. “How did we get to be so full of shit?” he asks his fellow Marines the morning after the dogfight before. “How did we become these fucking idiots?” View image in fullscreen Bad reputation … Phoenix in Stand by Me. Photograph: AJ Pics/Alamy If modern audiences want to know why Phoenix was so loved, said Ethan Hawke in 2014, “Go watch Stand By Me … James Dean has got nothing on that kid.” As the toughest but most complicated of the 12-year-old friends who trek into the woods to find a corpse in the late Rob Reiner’s film of Stephen King’s novella The Body, Phoenix evokes vividly the boy’s inner tensions, his hurt at the unfairness of his bad reputation; “I’d like to go some place where nobody knows me,” he sobs. Then there’s his exit. Each of the actor’s three greatest films gives him a killer final shot which has only gained in poignancy since his death.

chapters.label: 【篇章3】

paras.en: But it is his silent farewell in Stand by Me – waving at the camera, then plodding away and literally dissolving into thin air as the voiceover reveals that his character died prematurely – that hits the hardest. Phoenix received his only Oscar nomination for this fine drama about a pair of former radicals (Christine Lahti and Judd Hirsch) wanted by the FBI for their involvement in a bombing years earlier. He plays their eldest son, a sensitive piano prodigy who has learned never to let down his guard, which causes complications when he falls for his music teacher’s daughter (Plimpton). Under the direction of veteran auteur Sidney Lumet, who declared that Phoenix “couldn’t be ordinary if he tried”, the actor is achingly sad and true as the boy unfairly shouldering his parents’ burdens. It’s striking, too, that even in his short career, Phoenix starred in so many portraits of mysterious, idealistic and/ or itinerant families not unlike his own. This one, though, is the best. View image in fullscreen Bold … with Keanu Reeves in My Own Private Idaho. Photograph: Warner Bros Inc. Three decades ago, queer parts for straight-identifying actors were still thought of largely as awards bids (see William Hurt’s transparently covetous performance in Kiss of the Spider Woman) or career-killers (even at the end of the 1990s, Matt Damon, Brad Pitt and Leonardo DiCaprio all turned down Brokeback Mountain ). In that context, the boldness of Phoenix and Keanu Reeves in unselfconsciously playing sex workers in My Own Private Idaho, a kind of Midnight Cowboy cross-pollinated with Shakespeare’s Henry plays, should not be underestimated. But the narcoleptic hustler Mike, who turns tricks while searching for his mother, was no ordinary job for Phoenix.

“He was already this amazing actor,” said writer-director Gus Van Sant, “but with this film, he was able to have an effect on what the film was becoming … He was very excited he could control the destiny of his character.” The most obvious example is the campfire confession in which Mike admits his true feelings for Scott, the Prince Hal figure played by Reeves. The dialogue was scripted by Phoenix himself and scribbled on napkins, the scene moved to the end of the shoot so that he could build up to it emotionally. “The character I wrote was blasé and noncommittal,” said Van Sant. “River made him gay and committal; he redeemed him with emotions.” He did the same for the film, too. Van Sant’s innovative touches – shirtless studs coming to life on the covers of porn magazines, or the eerie pseudo-freeze-framed sex scenes – are cunning and cool, but it is Phoenix’s performance, from his opening orgasm to his final collapse on a deserted country road, that gives the movie its heart and its kick.

articles.title: ‘We crafted it from our hearts’: the Womack Sisters on continuing a great soul music dynasty

chapters.label: 【篇章1】

paras.en: ‘We’re committed’ … the Womack Sisters. Photograph: Rosie Cohe View image in fullscreen ‘We’re committed’ … the Womack Sisters. Photograph: Rosie Cohe Soul Interview ‘We crafted it from our hearts’: the Womack Sisters on continuing a great soul music dynasty Alexis Petridis Their parents were Womack & Womack, Uncle Bobby was a superstar and so was their grandfather, Sam Cooke. The trio explain how, after driving Ubers and being told soul was dead, they joined the family business Thu 6 Aug 2026 15. 30 BST Last modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 16. 57 BST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google B ackstage at a London festival, on a Sunday afternoon, the Womack Sisters are assembling themselves on a sofa, still clad in the clothes they were wearing on stage a few minutes ago. They look very stylish in their black dresses, tights and high heels, but they are not, it has to be said, dressed appropriately for the weather, which is sweltering. “You don’t feel anything on stage,” says Zeimani with a shrug. “You just feel amazing, like you’re floating.” “And we’re committed,” nods her sister BG. “You know, we were taught by professionals. ” View image in fullscreen Linda and Cecil Womack on stage in 1988. Photograph: Frans Schellekens/Redferns Indeed they were. BG, Zeimani and Kucha Womack’s father was Cecil Womack: he wrote Teddy Pendergrass’s oft-sampled classic Love TKO, as well as hits for the O’Jays, the Four Tops and Patti LaBelle , and was one half of Womack and Womack, of Love Wars and Teardrops fame. The other half was their mother, Linda Womack, the daughter of “king of soul” Sam Cooke.

Their uncle was Bobby Womack, who initially performed with Cecil in early-60s band the Valentinos – their most famous song was It’s All Over Now, later covered by the Rolling Stones – before going on to record a string of classics that earned him the unofficial soubriquet The Greatest Soul Singer in the World: from Across 110th Street to If You Think You’re Lonely Now to the triumphant final album he made before his death in 2014, The Bravest Man in the Universe. Their half-brother’s mum, meanwhile, was Mary “My Guy” Wells. Their mum and dad didn’t just take the kids along with them, they got them involved “in everything they did, in the studio, on stage, in meetings. They wanted to make sure that we knew what they were doing with their time, so they communicated with us a lot.” View image in fullscreen The Womack Sisters … ‘I could do this for the rest of my life!’

Photograph: Rosie Cohe BG says that if I had interviewed her parents back then, “We would have been in the interview. If they went on a television show, we were on the couch with them.” View image in fullscreen Conscience, featuring Zeimani. Photograph: Island Records Zeimani made her first public appearance as a baby, in her mother’s arms on the cover of Womack and Womack’s Conscience, the 1988 album featuring Teardrops. There was a cleaning company, and a brief stint, as Zeimani puts it, of “selling drugs”, which turns out to mean they ran a marijuana dispensary. But it wasn’t as easy as they had hoped. “We kept getting fired,” says BG. “I got fired from Zara for trying to take a couple of trips out of town for shows.” The sisters also drove Uber taxis. “Uber was a lifesaver! I swear, without it I would have been turning tricks,” BG laughs. View image in fullscreen ‘We crafted the album from our hearts.’ Photograph: Rosie Cohe To compound their problems, there was the music industry’s attitude towards them.

paras.en: The group “always had soul in mind,” says Zeimani – they were huge fans of Amy Winehouse – but the labels they met with kept pushing them towards pop. “We would go to them with our demos and tell them what we would like to accomplish, with a live band, an orchestra, everything. They were just like, ‘Soul’s not what’s happening right now, here in the States, particularly for brown artists.’ So for years we were trying other things. We dabbled in R&B. They even had us rapping a couple of times.” Hang on – are you saying you were told that Black artists shouldn’t make soul music? “Yeah, I know,” nods BG, rolling her eyes. “They told our manager that, and he didn’t want to tell us, he was so embarrassed. Eventually, we just put our foot down and said, ‘We’re not doing anything else.’ Couldn’t get anyone to invest in what we were doing, so we funded our own thing.” Happily, their own thing caught the attention of Daptone Records, home to Jalen Ngonda , Thee Sacred Souls and the late Sharon Jones , whose house band the Dap-Kings are best known for backing Winehouse on her Back to Black album. “An instant connection!” enthuses BG of their meeting with the label’s co-founder, Bosco Mann, who now plays bass in their backing band. “We just hung out and listened to music for a year before we actually recorded anything. So when we finally came down to it, it just rolled, it flowed, the music was just pouring out.”

The result was a string of acclaimed singles, among them Chauffeur – which details the downsides of the sisters’ period as Uber drivers, including realising that you’re invisible to the “fine-looking” man you just picked up – and If I Let You, which last month enjoyed a burst of social media virality after support from a startling array of luminaries: SZA, Timbaland, Ghostface Killah, Pharrell Williams, Erykah Badu and Questlove. One suspects the stars were drawn by the Womack Sisters’ fusion of traditional and modern: the music on their upcoming debut album is as deeply rooted in soul’s past as you’d expect (“We are,” as Kucha puts it, “so familiar with these streets”), but it never feels self-consciously retro. But it does feel strikingly raw, racked with very real emotion. “We crafted it from our hearts,” says Zeimani. “I wouldn’t say that we had a lot of sorrow to get off our chests, but there is a lot of relationship drama in our family, you know? Our father passed away, our Uncle Bob passed away shortly afterwards. Our aunt, our Uncle Jude’s wife, there was a car accident and she didn’t make it. I lost my husband in Atlanta in 2020 – he was robbed, he got shot, he didn’t survive. You find love, there’s nothing that impacts you more, and to lose it before you can fully experience it – like, we were married but we were about to start a family … I had a really hard time moving through that. “You know how when we were in the pandemic, we couldn’t do anything? That’s really what you need to do to reset from loss – stop doing everything, just love on yourself, go to the beach, find a reason to smile again.”

View image in fullscreen The Womack clan … top (L-R), Bobby, Curtis and Harry; bottom (L-R), Friendly Sr, Friendly Jr and Cecil. Photograph: Michael Ochs Archives/Getty Images Their live shows, meanwhile, are proving triumphant. At the London festival, their set featured a roaring take on Teardrops, their parents’ most enduring hit. No, they say, they aren’t intimidated by their family’s legacy. “We’re proud of them, but they exist in their own right. The time they came up in and the things they faced – segregation, things we can’t even imagine – they saw that,” says Zeimani. “If you can imagine, our mother came up behind Sam Cooke – and we saw her win Grammys,” nods Kucha. “So I’m just like, well, she did it.” “She focused on herself – that was her advice to us,” says Zeimani. “And Uncle Bob’s career was piping hot at the same time as my dad’s career was piping hot, so we saw that we could coexist without competing, because they were very different from one another. They always told us: you’re not us and you don’t have to be. You’re you, and there’ll never be anyone like you. We took that seriously.” The Womack Sisters is released 14 August via Daptone

articles.title: From here on out?
articles.text:
Please explain “from here on out” in this sentence: He’s told to cut back on alcohol from here on out.

This man (he) got drunk and made a fool of himself probably. Either that or too much alcohol has caused his health to deteriorate.

Hence, he’s told by someone, perhaps a doctor, to, from now on, drink less and mind his health more.

“From here on out” means from now on, starting from here, this place and point, going forward.

“From here on out” is a variation of the more commonplace phrase “from here on” or “from now on”. “Here” refers to this place whereas “now” refers to the present time. “Here and now”, which is actually a phrase, means exactly what it says, here – and now – as a starting point.

In other words, he’s told to cut back on alcohol right here and now, without delay.

“Out” suggests this advice is permanent, lasting forever – till time runs “out”, if you will.

In other words, no return back to binge drinking, ever.

To sum up, in short, “from here on out” is the same as “from here on” or “from now on” but perhaps is more emphatic-sounding.

Let’s read the following media examples to see for yourself whether “from here on out” does sound more emphatic:

1. Postseason expectations are slipping away with each loss for the Cincinnati Bengals.

Heading into Sunday with a 3-5 record, Joe Burrow knows his squad can’t afford anymore losses.

Thus, be it only Week 9 or not, Burrow has deemed the Bengals’ matchup against the Las Vegas Raiders the must-win variety.

“This is a must-win game,” Burrow told reporters Wednesday. “We’re 3-5. You go to 3-6, then you gotta basically win out to get in. Urgency’s very high every week from here on out.”

Having stumbled out to a 0-3 start to the season, the Bengals briefly found their stride with three victories in four games – all against losing teams. However, Cincinnati’s first four losses were all by six points or less. Now, the Bengals must rebound from a 37-17 loss to the Philadelphia Eagles.

A team predicted by many to claim the AFC North and some to make the Super Bowl, the Bengals are entrenched in the reality of their status. And there's no time to think about woulda, coulda, shoulda at this point.

“This is the situation that we find ourselves in,” Burrow said. “We know what we have to do going forward, and we’re going to attack that challenge to the best of our ability. And try to give ourselves the best chance to win with my play and try to continue to be as consistent as I can and try to find a win.”

- Joe Burrow tabs Bengals’ game vs. Raiders ‘must-win’: ‘Urgency’s very high every week from here on out’, October 30, 2024.

2. The Penguin’s Colin Farrell took home a Golden Globe for “Best Male Actor in a Limited Series,” after continuing his role as Oz Cobb/The Penguin from The Batman. During his acceptance speech, the star opened with a joke: “No one to thank on this when I did it all by myself – just a raw, pared-away performance.” Immediately after his quip, Farrell added that he had “too many people to thank” and that “it takes a village, whether it’s on the small screen or the big screen.”

Among those the actor shouted out were showrunner Lauren LeFranc, costar Cristin Milioti, and The Batman director, Matt Reeves, quipping that the latter would “kill [him] if [he doesn’t] thank him.” Farrell was quick to credit everyone else who worked on The Batman and The Penguin for his success: “I’m here on the backs of the talents of so many people through the years.”

More specifically, Farrell also thanked the hair and makeup team responsible for his transformation into the Penguin, led by Mike Marino. Per the star, “all it took was three hours in the chair in the morning. I drank black coffee, listened to ’80s music and I became a canvas for that team’s brilliance.” In an especially kind move, Farrell noted that the production was also supported by departments like craft services, which provided food and refreshments for the cast and crew, saying they “kept the whole crew going.”

While Farrell made a careful note to thank many who contributed to his role as the Penguin, he drew special attention to his appreciation of Matt Reeves. Given that he originated his time as Oz in Reeves’ The Batman and that Reeves executive produced The Penguin, this extra emphasis makes sense. Reeves is in large part responsible for casting Farrell, though the actor still deserves credit for the gravitas he brought to the Penguin character. Interestingly, Farrell thanking Reeves also reminds audiences that there will be more of Oz to come in The Batman Part II.

During his speech, the actor also joked: “I guess it’s prosthetics from here on out.” While this comment was cheeky in nature, it indicates a clear interest in continuing his tenure as the Penguin.

- Colin Farrell Thanks The Batman Director After Golden Globes Win And Addresses His Role As The Penguin, ScreenRant.com, January 6, 2025.

3. Late-night hosts took aim at the ineffective tactics of the Democrats while also taking issue with Donald Trump’s response to the weekend’s deadly storms.

On The Daily Show, Jon Stewart said that “it is Trump’s world and we’re just cowering in it” in a segment devoted to calling out how poorly the Democrats have handled his second presidency.

Over the weekend, Trump played golf once again, which led to a picture of him walking into an office “in his golf attire to bomb the shit out of Yemen”. In attacking the country he “continued a presidential tradition going back decades”.

With the recent vote over the new Republican budget to avoid a shutdown, Democrats finally had “an opportunity to stand up” to a “wannabe tyrant”.

The budget was criticized by some as a non-starter yet Chuck Schumer broke ranks and voted to move it forward. “What the fuck happened?” he asked.

On Jimmy Kimmel Live! the host said that on St Patrick’s Day it was “nice to have an excuse to drink on a Monday” given how bad things currently are.

There was “a terrible weekend of deadly storms” yet the president who chided Joe Biden for being away when Hurricane Helene raged decided to play golf once again. “If you scored hypocrisy like golf he’d be 30 strokes under par right now,” he said.

Please explain “from here on out” in this sentence: He’s told to cut back on alcohol from here on out.

This man (he) got drunk and made a fool of himself probably. Either that or too much alcohol has caused his health to deteriorate.

Hence, he’s told by someone, perhaps a doctor, to, from now on, drink less and mind his health more.

“From here on out” means from now on, starting from here, this place and point, going forward.

“From here on out” is a variation of the more commonplace phrase “from here on” or “from now on”. “Here” refers to this place whereas “now” refers to the present time. “Here and now”, which is actually a phrase, means exactly what it says, here – and now – as a starting point.

In other words, he’s told to cut back on alcohol right here and now, without delay.

“Out” suggests this advice is permanent, lasting forever – till time runs “out”, if you will.

In other words, no return back to binge drinking, ever.

To sum up, in short, “from here on out” is the same as “from here on” or “from now on” but perhaps is more emphatic-sounding.

Let’s read the following media examples to see for yourself whether “from here on out” does sound more emphatic:

1. Postseason expectations are slipping away with each loss for the Cincinnati Bengals.

Heading into Sunday with a 3-5 record, Joe Burrow knows his squad can’t afford anymore losses.

Thus, be it only Week 9 or not, Burrow has deemed the Bengals’ matchup against the Las Vegas Raiders the must-win variety.

“This is a must-win game,” Burrow told reporters Wednesday. “We’re 3-5. You go to 3-6, then you gotta basically win out to get in. Urgency’s very high every week from here on out.”

Having stumbled out to a 0-3 start to the season, the Bengals briefly found their stride with three victories in four games – all against losing teams. However, Cincinnati’s first four losses were all by six points or less. Now, the Bengals must rebound from a 37-17 loss to the Philadelphia Eagles.

A team predicted by many to claim the AFC North and some to make the Super Bowl, the Bengals are entrenched in the reality of their status. And there's no time to think about woulda, coulda, shoulda at this point.

“This is the situation that we find ourselves in,” Burrow said. “We know what we have to do going forward, and we’re going to attack that challenge to the best of our ability. And try to give ourselves the best chance to win with my play and try to continue to be as consistent as I can and try to find a win.”

- Joe Burrow tabs Bengals’ game vs. Raiders ‘must-win’: ‘Urgency’s very high every week from here on out’, October 30, 2024.

2. The Penguin’s Colin Farrell took home a Golden Globe for “Best Male Actor in a Limited Series,” after continuing his role as Oz Cobb/The Penguin from The Batman. During his acceptance speech, the star opened with a joke: “No one to thank on this when I did it all by myself – just a raw, pared-away performance.” Immediately after his quip, Farrell added that he had “too many people to thank” and that “it takes a village, whether it’s on the small screen or the big screen.”

Among those the actor shouted out were showrunner Lauren LeFranc, costar Cristin Milioti, and The Batman director, Matt Reeves, quipping that the latter would “kill [him] if [he doesn’t] thank him.” Farrell was quick to credit everyone else who worked on The Batman and The Penguin for his success: “I’m here on the backs of the talents of so many people through the years.”

More specifically, Farrell also thanked the hair and makeup team responsible for his transformation into the Penguin, led by Mike Marino. Per the star, “all it took was three hours in the chair in the morning. I drank black coffee, listened to ’80s music and I became a canvas for that team’s brilliance.” In an especially kind move, Farrell noted that the production was also supported by departments like craft services, which provided food and refreshments for the cast and crew, saying they “kept the whole crew going.”

While Farrell made a careful note to thank many who contributed to his role as the Penguin, he drew special attention to his appreciation of Matt Reeves. Given that he originated his time as Oz in Reeves’ The Batman and that Reeves executive produced The Penguin, this extra emphasis makes sense. Reeves is in large part responsible for casting Farrell, though the actor still deserves credit for the gravitas he brought to the Penguin character. Interestingly, Farrell thanking Reeves also reminds audiences that there will be more of Oz to come in The Batman Part II.

During his speech, the actor also joked: “I guess it’s prosthetics from here on out.” While this comment was cheeky in nature, it indicates a clear interest in continuing his tenure as the Penguin.

- Colin Farrell Thanks The Batman Director After Golden Globes Win And Addresses His Role As The Penguin, ScreenRant.com, January 6, 2025.

3. Late-night hosts took aim at the ineffective tactics of the Democrats while also taking issue with Donald Trump’s response to the weekend’s deadly storms.

On The Daily Show, Jon Stewart said that “it is Trump’s world and we’re just cowering in it” in a segment devoted to calling out how poorly the Democrats have handled his second presidency.

Over the weekend, Trump played golf once again, which led to a picture of him walking into an office “in his golf attire to bomb the shit out of Yemen”. In attacking the country he “continued a presidential tradition going back decades”.

With the recent vote over the new Republican budget to avoid a shutdown, Democrats finally had “an opportunity to stand up” to a “wannabe tyrant”.

The budget was criticized by some as a non-starter yet Chuck Schumer broke ranks and voted to move it forward. “What the fuck happened?” he asked.

There was “a terrible weekend of deadly storms” yet the president who chided Joe Biden for being away when Hurricane Helene raged decided to play golf once again. “If you scored hypocrisy like golf he’d be 30 strokes under par right now,” he said.

Trump claimed victory again but Kimmel asked: “Who are the other players in this tournament?”

He joked that it could just be “Eric with his Fisher Price clubs” and demanded “a forensic investigation” into the game.

Later that day, Trump finally posted that he would be praying with Melania for those affected. “Praying together might be the only activity those two do less than sleeping together,” Kimmel joked.

This weekend also saw Trump get accidentally prodded by a fuzzy microphone during an interview. “How funny would it be if that happened every time he was interviewed from here on out?” he joked.

- Jon Stewart on Democrats: ‘It’s Trump’s world and we’re just cowering in it’, TheGuardian.com, March 18, 2025.
